prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker is forced to climb a ladder under threat of being buried alive in foamy mud.
- After being hanged from a tree, the speaker is thrown into a stream and drifts to a village where someone prays for their soul.
- The poem presents death as having endless possible forms but rejects the idea that it is simply a lullaby about the world’s end.
- It focuses instead on bodily decay in daylight, describing insects, parasites, dogs, ghosts, and rats consuming the dead.
- The children are told to sing softly and lovingly in order to avoid “the hole.”
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

Through a nightmarish first-person account of forced execution, decomposition, and predation, the poem uses grotesque imagery and a distorted lullaby form to explore death and terror. It concludes that children must answer the threat of annihilation by singing with tenderness and love, suggesting art as a fragile means of resistance and survival.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: They, The

outputs.L1:
They took my body into the forest.  
They ordered me to climb a ladder.  
I did not want to climb,  
but they forced me.

“If you do not climb the ladder,  
we will bury you in the foamy mud.”

I had to decide:  
Should I die by hanging  
or by burial?

I climbed the ladder,  
and they wrapped a belt  
around the thick limb of a tree.

Then, when I could no longer breathe,  
they tossed me into a stream.

I floated to the edge of the village,  
where someone prayed for my soul.

It is like this in a lullaby  
for the end of the world:  
the possibilities for the end  
are endless.

But this is not truly a lullaby  
for the end of the world.

It is about the beginning—  
what happens when we begin to rot  
in the daylight;

the way the light falls upon  
the ants, worms, and parasites  
mauling our bodies;

the swarms of dogs  
gnawing at our skin and bones.

Do you know what it is like  
when a ghost licks your intestines?

Do you know what it is like  
when a rat devours your brain?

To avoid the hole,  
the children must sing sweetly, softly.

To avoid the hole,  
they must fill their songs with love.
outputs.L2:
They carried my remains into the woods  
and ordered me up the rungs.  
I resisted, unwilling to ascend,  
but they gave me no choice.  

“Refuse,” they said,  
“and we’ll cover you beneath frothing mire.”  
So I faced two deaths:  
the noose or the grave.  

I went up.  
They looped a strap over a heavy tree branch,  
and after my breath had been cut away,  
they threw me into running water.  

The current bore me toward the village boundary,  
where a stranger offered a prayer for my spirit.  

This might sound like a cradle song  
sung as the world expires—  
a song reminding us  
that destruction can take countless forms.  

Yet it is not truly about the world’s conclusion.  
It concerns the moment things commence:  
the decay that unfolds beneath the sun,  
light falling across ants, worms, and other parasites  
as they ravage our flesh.  

It tells of packs of dogs  
chewing through skin and bone.  
Can you imagine a phantom  
dragging its tongue over your entrails?  
Can you imagine a rodent  
feeding upon your brain?  

If the children wish to escape the pit,  
they must sing in gentle, tender voices.  
To remain outside the grave,  
they must make every song overflow with love.
outputs.L3:
The speaker is forced to climb a ladder under the threat of being buried alive in foamy mud. After being hanged from a tree, they are thrown into a stream and carried by the current toward a village, where someone offers a prayer for their soul. Through this sequence of violent and surreal images, the poem suggests that death can assume an endless variety of forms. At the same time, it rejects the comforting notion that death is merely a lullaby marking the end of the world.

Instead, the poem confronts the physical reality of death in stark daylight. It emphasizes bodily decay, depicting insects, parasites, dogs, ghosts, and rats feeding on or consuming the dead. These disturbing images strip death of sentimentality and present it as a process of exposure, decomposition, and disappearance. Against this grim vision, the children are urged to sing softly and lovingly, as though tenderness itself might offer protection and help them avoid “the hole”—an image that evokes the grave, annihilation, or an inescapable fate.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents death through a nightmarish first-person account in which the speaker is subjected to forced execution, bodily decomposition, and eventual predation. By allowing the victim to narrate these experiences directly, the poem makes terror feel immediate and inescapable. Grotesque images of physical destruction collapse the boundary between the human body and the natural world: the body becomes flesh, food, and matter, stripped of dignity by violence. This transformation conveys not only the horror of death but also the fear of erasure—the possibility that a person may be reduced to an object and disappear without meaning or remembrance.

The poem’s form intensifies this disturbing effect. It resembles a lullaby or children’s song, genres normally associated with comfort, innocence, and protection, yet its rhythms and images are filled with menace. This distortion turns something familiar and soothing into something uncanny. The contrast suggests that violence has invaded even the protected world of childhood, making ordinary forms of reassurance inadequate. Repetition and songlike language do not calm the reader; instead, they mimic the circular, obsessive quality of fear and trauma.

Despite its grim imagery, however, the poem does not end in complete despair. Its final appeal to children—to sing with tenderness and love—offers a fragile response to the threat of annihilation. The children cannot necessarily defeat death or undo violence, but they can refuse the emotional brutality that violence attempts to impose. Their song preserves compassion, memory, and human connection in a world that seeks to destroy them.

Art therefore becomes a modest but meaningful form of resistance. Singing cannot guarantee physical survival, yet it can protect something essential: the ability to feel, to care, and to give suffering a voice. By transforming terror into song, the poem suggests that tenderness itself can be defiant. Love and artistic expression do not erase death, but they prevent death from having the final word.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse horror poem about execution, decay, and children singing to escape death, framed as a “lullaby for the end of the world.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Lullaby for the End of the World**

Hush now—  
the gallows are counting  
each breath in the square.

One for the rope,  
two for the chair,  
three for the blade  
with its moon-white stare.

The condemned stand barefoot  
where the garden once grew,  
their names sewn shut  
in the mouths of the living.

Above them, bells rot in their towers.  
Below, the earth practices hunger.

And still the children sing.

Not loudly—  
death is a bird  
that startles at joy—  
but low in their throats,  
a thread through a needle,  
a door drawn in dust:

*Sleep, little fire,*  
*sleep under stone.*  
*When the dark comes to count us,*  
*say no one is home.*

The houses lean inward, listening.  
Milk sours in sealed bottles.  
Photographs soften with mold  
until every mother wears  
the same green face.

At dawn, the executioner  
washes his hands in rainwater.  
By noon, the rain has teeth.  
By evening, the dead  
are opening like black flowers.

And still the children sing,

because the song makes a room  
where no room remains,  
because each note is a stair  
the grave cannot climb,  
because terror, too, must pause  
to remember the words.

*Sleep, little bone,*  
*sleep, little breath.*  
*We will sing past the soldiers,*  
*we will sing past death.*

One voice falters.  
Another carries it.

One candle gutters.  
A hundred small mouths  
become flame.

The world ends badly—  
not with trumpets,  
but with the wet collapse of roofs,  
the soft industry of worms,  
the final rope swinging  
after its burden is gone.

Yet under the ruins,  
under ash, under iron,  
under the blind machinery  
still warm from killing,

the lullaby continues—

thin as a pulse,  
stubborn as grass  
between the teeth of a skull:

*Hush now, hush.*  
*The night cannot stay.*  
*If we sing until morning,*  
*there must be a day.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a disturbing surrealist poem in the voice of a murdered person whose body is hanged, thrown into a stream, and consumed by animals and parasites.
counterfactuals.output:
They taught my neck the grammar of rope,  
a hard little alphabet of knots,  
and left me conjugating the wind  
above a field of blind wheat.

All night, the moon wore my face  
like a stolen coin.  
My shoes filled with moths.  
My shadow kicked the earth  
but could not wake it.

At dawn they cut me down  
and the world climbed backward through my eyes.  
They carried me gently—  
as men carry a mirror  
after it has witnessed them—

then gave me to the stream.

Water entered every locked room.  
It combed my hair with reeds,  
buttoned me into a coat of mud,  
and whispered: *No one stays one person.*

I drifted beneath bridges  
where children dreamed upstream.  
My hands opened like pale lilies.  
Small fish moved through my sleeves  
as if searching a drowned house  
for something still warm.

On the bank, the fox found me.  
It took my silence first.  
Crows unstitched the weather from my skin.  
Beetles polished their black prayers  
inside the chapel of my ribs.

Then came the patient nations:  
the larvae, the mites, the pale  
and eyeless citizens of ending.  
They made a country of me.  
They raised soft flags in my mouth.  
They ate my name down to its roots.

Now I speak from everywhere—

from the crow’s bright hunger,  
from the fox asleep beneath thorn,  
from the silver bellies of fish,  
from the stream rehearsing my murder  
over every stone.

Do not search for my body.

The rope keeps only my question.  
The water keeps only my shape.  
The animals carry me into the forest  
piece by dreaming piece.

And under the soil,  
what remains of my voice  
is learning to bloom  
with its teeth still in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an apocalyptic prose poem that begins with someone being forced to climb a ladder in a forest and ends with children singing sweetly to avoid a burial hole.
counterfactuals.output:
They forced me to climb a ladder in the forest, though it leaned against nothing but rain. Below, the soldiers wore masks of bark and bone; above, the last birds circled a sun gone black at the edges. Each rung hummed with the names of vanished towns. Each time I looked down, the earth had opened wider, showing its red roots and the pale machinery buried beneath them, still turning after the end of power, still manufacturing keys for doors that no longer existed.

At the top, I stepped into the sky.

There I found the ruined world spread like a scorched map: rivers steaming in their beds, cathedrals full of wolves, highways braided with weeds and abandoned shoes. The cities had become enormous clocks, all stopped at the same minute. From their towers poured ash, slow and ceremonial, softening the shoulders of statues, filling the mouths of bells.

A voice inside the clouds instructed us to repent, but no one remembered the proper language. The survivors gathered in supermarkets and whispered apologies to empty shelves. Mothers swaddled stones. Fathers planted photographs in the fields. At night, the moon came close enough to reveal its cracks, and through those cracks shone a terrible blue fire.

By winter, the sea had learned to walk. It crossed the plains carrying ships on its back, knocking gently at every house. The dead rose only in dreams, asking whether morning had returned. We lied and said yes. We lied until the word *morning* became warm again.

Then the digging began.

In every village, one person was chosen to hold the shovel and another to hold the lantern. No one spoke of what waited under the soil, breathing patiently through layers of root and rust. We only listened as the ground counted backward.

And in the final settlement, beneath a sky crowded with falling stars, the children stood hand in hand at the edge of the dark, singing sweetly to avoid a burial hole.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, visceral anti-lullaby exploring the endless ways people die and what happens to their bodies afterward. Include ghosts, rats, dogs, ants, worms, and a repeated refrain about avoiding “the hole.”
counterfactuals.output:
Hush now, darling, bolt the door,  
Death keeps count beneath the floor.  
Some go softly, some go loud,  
Some beneath a falling crowd.  
Some in fever, some in flame,  
Some leave nothing but a name.  

**Don’t go down, don’t lose your soul—  
Run from the dark, avoid the hole.  
Nail up the night, swallow it whole:  
Run, little heartbeat—avoid the hole.**

Ghosts press faces to the glass,  
Mouthing warnings as you pass.  
Rats stitch tunnels through the wall,  
Patient for the last footfall.  
Dogs will nose the frozen ground,  
Whine where missing bones are found.  

Some are sunk beneath the foam,  
Far from kin and far from home.  
Some lie pale in antiseptic light,  
Tagged and wheeled away at night.  
Some are ash in urns of clay;  
Some feed roots and fade away.  

**Don’t go down, don’t lose your soul—  
Run from the dark, avoid the hole.  
Hold to the bell while ravens toll:  
Run, little heartbeat—avoid the hole.**

Ants come marching, grain by grain,  
Through the mouth and through the rain.  
Worms know nothing—worms don’t grieve;  
They take whatever we must leave.  
Skin gives way and sinews part;  
Earth makes mud of lung and heart.  

Coffins buckle, grave clothes rot,  
Names wear thin and dates are forgot.  
Teeth stay quiet, white and small,  
Long after kings and kingdoms fall.  
Ghosts drift hungry, thin as smoke,  
Still repeating words they spoke.  

**Don’t go down, don’t lose your soul—  
Run from the dark, avoid the hole.  
Cling to the dawn, though night takes toll:  
Run, little heartbeat—avoid the hole.**

Hush now, darling, morning’s near.  
Every cradle casts a bier.  
Yet while the blood still drums its tune,  
Spit at earth and curse the moon.  
Death has roads beyond control—  
So bar the gate.

**Avoid the hole.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an experimental poem with minimal punctuation and stark line breaks, combining forced execution, decomposition in daylight, grotesque rhetorical questions, and an eerie final image of children filling their songs with love.
counterfactuals.output:
At noon they fasten the sentence  
around his wrists  

the rifles lift  
like a row of blind windows  

who taught the sun  
to watch without blinking  

the body opens its dark republic  
to flies  
to heat  
to the patient green mouths  

is this justice  
with its teeth full of summer  

is this mercy  
wearing another mans face  

by evening  
the shadow has left him  
but the light keeps eating  

beyond the wall  
children gather dust in their hair  

and fill their songs  
with love
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
